column1: # iota(4,11) >= 32 ?  the deg(0) = 13 cube under cryptominisat5, over the
# FULL degree-sequence split, one line per sub-cube.  Second opinion for
# cadical's UNSAT at 85123.9 s (docs/ladder/iota4_11.tsv).
# Written by `iota_sym --checkpoint`; a row is appended the moment a
# sub-cube lands, so a reclaimed container loses only what was in flight.
# Resume with the same --checkpoint: UNSAT/SAT rows are skipped, UNKNOWN
# rows are re-run, because UNKNOWN is a budget and not a verdict.
# all_points_used = FALSE, so THE CUBE IS UNSAT ONLY WHEN ALL 1949
# SUB-CUBES ARE UNSAT.  This is NOT the same cover as
# docs/ladder/iota4_11.deg13.tsv, which holds 1939 -- that file was
# written through tools/rung.sh, which passes --ladder and so asks for a
# family on EXACTLY eleven points.  This run was launched from the binary
# without --ladder, so it asks for one on AT MOST eleven points: a
# strictly larger cover, 1939 of it shared and ten more carrying a
# degree-zero point.  UNSAT on all 1949 implies UNSAT on all 1939, so
# this is a sound second opinion and a slightly stronger one; the ten
# extras are redundant, being refuted already by iota(4,10) = 27 < 32.
# Do not merge rows between the two files.  See roadmap 52.1.
# Command:
#   iota_sym 4 11 32 --only-deg 13 --solver cryptominisat5 \
#     --seqprefix 11 --cubecap 2000 --slice 60 --seconds 5400 --threads 4 \
#     --checkpoint docs/ladder/iota4_11.deg13.cryptominisat5.tsv
# THE SECONDS COLUMN IS WALL TIME UNDER CONTENTION and is not comparable
# with the cadical rows in iota4_11.deg13.tsv.  This ran on a 4-core
# session container alongside `cargo test --release` and `make verify`,
# and rows recording 664-820 s against a 600 s solver budget are the
# measure of that, not of the sub-cube.  Same caveat as roadmap 40.2.
# Why the full split and not the prefix-3 split that roadmap 50.3 asked
# for: the prefix-3 split of this cube is 27 sub-cubes, and the four ever
# attempted (under cadical, iota4_11.deg13.p3.tsv) all burned 2400 s
# without landing.  Those four are the first four in lexicographically
# descending enumeration order, covering 553, 325, 180 and 94 full
# sub-cubes -- 1152 of 1939, three fifths of the cube in four pieces.  At
# the 136-491 s a full sub-cube costs, the largest is ~10^5 s of search,
# so a 7200 s budget banks nothing.  The full split is what
# iota4_11.deg13.tsv calls the working granularity.  See roadmap 52.2.
# TWO PASSES, AND THE ROW COUNT IS NOT THE CUBE COUNT.  A 600 s pass ran
# first and banked 3 UNSAT of 20 attempted; an 1800 s pass then resumed
# against this same file, which skipped those 3 and re-ran the 17 UNKNOWN
# ones -- "checkpoint: 3 of 1949 cubes already decided".  The 600 s cap
# was too small for this solver: cryptominisat5 landed 1 of the 8
# sub-cubes it shares with cadical's pass, where cadical landed 5, so
# 600 s here is about a 200 s cadical-equivalent.
# TEN CONTAINER RESTARTS ABSORBED, ZERO ROWS LOST.  The sixth was at
# ~17:53 UTC, the seventh at ~21:36, the eighth at ~22:00, the ninth at
# ~22:05 and the tenth at ~03:32; each killed the driver and all four
# solvers mid-flight.  Every time the same command printed
# "checkpoint: 129 of 1949 cubes already decided" and resumed -- a number
# that matches an independent recount of the distinct UNSAT labels in
# this file, which is the check that makes "zero rows lost" a verified
# statement and not a hope.  Every banked UNSAT survived; the only work
# lost is the partial search in the four solvers that were running,
# which is bounded by the cap.
# **This is the entire argument for the degree-sequence split over the
# whole-cube monolith, and it is now demonstrated ten times rather
# than argued once** -- the monolith has twice been killed at ~85000 s
# and lost everything, because a single instance has nothing to check
# point.
# **AND THE RESTART CADENCE HAS BECOME THE BINDING CONSTRAINT ON
# PROGRESS, WHICH IS A DIFFERENT PROBLEM FROM LOSING ROWS.**  No row has
# ever been lost, and that is not the issue.  The issue is arithmetic
# between two numbers:
#     to reach ANY fresh sub-cube the resume policy must first re-run
#     all ten stragglers, ten attempts over four threads at a 10800 s
#     cap = three batches = ABOUT 7.5 UNINTERRUPTED WALL-HOURS;
#     observed gaps between the last six restarts:
#         5th ->  6th  12 h 57 m     long enough
#         6th ->  7th   3 h 43 m     not enough
#         7th ->  8th      24 m      not enough
#         8th ->  9th       5 m      not enough for ANY attempt at all
#         9th -> 10th   5 h 27 m     not enough for the sweep, but the
#                                    run banked four rows inside it
# A restart resets the sweep to its beginning -- after the eighth AND
# the ninth the driver went straight back to c59/c67/c68/c70, the same
# four the sixth and seventh had started on.  **While the gap stays
# below about 7.5 hours this run re-runs stragglers forever and never
# attempts a fresh sub-cube again**, banking nothing while looking
# perfectly healthy: driver up, four solvers busy, no errors.  That
# failure mode is invisible from the process list, which is why it is
# written here.
# **THE PREVIOUS PARAGRAPH'S OWN CAVEAT IS NOW WITHDRAWN.**  One batch
# ago this said "two-restarts-in-24-minutes is a sample of one gap; do
# not conclude the cadence has permanently changed".  That caution was
# right to write and is now overtaken: the very next gap was FIVE
# MINUTES.  Three consecutive gaps -- 3 h 43 m, 24 m, 5 m -- are all
# below the 7.5 hours the sweep needs, and the last is below the 3 h a
# SINGLE straggler attempt needs, so nothing at all can now complete.
# The run is not progressing; it is being restarted.
# STILL NOT ACTED ON, AND THE OPTIONS ARE WRITTEN DOWN RATHER THAN
# CHOSEN.  Each changes the experiment, so each is a decision and not a
# repair:
#   (a) accept it and keep restarting -- costs nothing, banks nothing
#       while the cadence holds;
#   (b) lower `--seconds` so an attempt fits inside the observed uptime.
#       This CHANGES THE CAP, which the budget rule governs, and would
#       mix rows measured at different caps into one file -- the exact
#       confusion 52.1 and 50.3 were about;
#   (c) change the resume order so fresh cubes are attempted before
#       straggler repeats.  Cheap sub-cubes have landed in 300-2400 s
#       and would fit inside even a 24 m window, so this is the option
#       that would actually bank rows -- but it is a change under
#       `rust/`, which this branch has not touched since 105b00e0, and
#       that untouched tree is what the gates argument in the PR body
#       rests on.
# Flagged for a decision rather than made quietly.
# **THE TENTH RESTART WAS THE EXPENSIVE ONE, AND THE REASON IS WHEN IT
# LANDED RATHER THAN WHAT IT KILLED.**  Batch 2 of the sweep started at
# 00:55-01:08 on c71, c95, c96 and c97; the restart came at ~03:32, so
# those four solvers died about 2 h 25 m into a 3 h cap -- roughly 85%
# of the way through, against the seventh restart's 40 minutes, or 22%.
# Same four cubes, same cap, more than three times the wall time thrown
# away: about ten solver-hours here against two and a half there.
# **The expected yield lost is nonetheless small, and the two numbers
# should not be confused.**  Every remaining straggler is run>=12 <= 7,
# where the observed repeat yield is 1 of 23, so those four attempts were
# worth about 0.17 UNSAT between them however far they had got.  A
# restart's cost in WALL TIME depends sharply on when in the batch it
# lands; its cost in EXPECTED ROWS does not, because an attempt that is
# 85% finished has banked exactly as much as one that is 22% finished,
# which is nothing.  That asymmetry is the whole reason a checkpoint at
# sub-cube granularity is worth having, and it is also why "we lost ten
# solver-hours" and "we lost a sixth of an UNSAT" are both true here.
# WHAT THE SEVENTH RESTART ACTUALLY COST, WHICH IS LESS THAN "FOUR
# SOLVERS' WORK" SOUNDS.  Both the sixth and the seventh landed while
# the resume policy was re-running stragglers, so what was in flight
# both times was straggler repeats -- at the seventh, cubes c71, c95,
# c96 and c97, about forty minutes into a 10800 s cap.  At the measured
# 0.11 per repeat those four attempts carried an expected yield of
# about 0.44 UNSAT, and they were forty minutes of the way to earning
# it.  The loss is real but it is small, and it is smaller than the
# same interruption would have been against fresh sub-cubes.  Recorded
# because "killed four solvers mid-flight" invites overestimating the
# damage, and the number is available rather than guessed at.
# NOTE ON RESTART: phase one re-runs the WHOLE deg(0) = 13 cube for one
# --slice (60 s) before re-splitting.  On a fresh start you will see a
# solver on `sf-sym-11-4-32-c0-...`, with no `seq` in the name, and the
# split only appears a minute later on `...-seq-cNN-...`.  That is not a
# regression to the monolith; it is `plan_phase_two`.  Wait for the
# "checkpoint: N of 1949" line before concluding anything.
# `append_checkpoint` appends unconditionally and never dedups, so a
# re-run leaves the old UNKNOWN row in place beside the new one.  Rows are
# therefore >= cubes attempted, and a label may appear more than once.
# Only UNSAT/SAT rows are load-bearing, and those are written once; to
# count progress, count DISTINCT labels with an UNSAT verdict.
# WHAT THE 1800 s PASS BOUGHT, measured.  Its UNSAT rows land between
# 740.5 s and 1588.7 s -- all above the 600 s cap that had left them
# UNKNOWN, all under 1800 s.  So 600 s was cutting off sub-cubes this
# solver can decide, and the first pass's budget was largely wasted on
# them.  Two sub-cubes are still UNKNOWN at 1800 s, and the largest UNSAT
# used 88% of that budget, so a third pass at a larger cap would likely
# still gain -- it is not yet at the point of diminishing returns.
# STANDING, 21 distinct UNSAT of 42 labels attempted, 0 SAT.
# EVERY SUB-CUBE CADICAL EVER RECORDED FOR THIS CUBE IS NOW DECIDED, AND
# THE TWO SOLVERS AGREE ON ALL OF THEM.  cadical's pass attempted
# fourteen and landed five, leaving nine UNKNOWN at its 600 s cap.
# cryptominisat5 is UNSAT on all fourteen -- the five it confirms, and
# all nine cadical could not decide:
# So the portion of cube 13 that any solver has examined is now fully
# decided and fully agreed.  Seven further sub-cubes are decided beyond
# cadical's fourteen.
# THIS DOES NOT DECIDE THE CUBE.  21 of 1949 is 1%, and iota(4,11) <= 31
# still rests on cadical's whole-cube UNSAT at 85123.9 s.  What it
# removes is the possibility that cadical's nine UNKNOWNs were hiding a
# SAT: they were not, and a SAT among them would have contradicted that
# whole-cube verdict.
#     0   DISAGREEMENTS throughout.  No SAT anywhere, in 68 rows.
# STANDING: 154 UNSAT, 0 UNKNOWN, 0 SAT over 154 labels -- 154 of 1949,
# 259 rows.  (This lead read "131 UNSAT, 8 UNKNOWN over 139 labels" while
# the sentence two lines below it already said 146 and 0 -- stale from the
# batch that introduced the sweep-complete line and not re-derived since.
# Corrected by recounting from the rows; logged in 54.3a.)
# **THE SWEEP IS COMPLETE, THE RUN IS BANKING FRESH SUB-CUBES,
# AND THE ENUMERATION HAS MOVED TO THE PREDICTED NEXT GROUP.**  153
# UNSAT, 0 UNKNOWN, 0 SAT over 153 labels -- every label ever attempted
# is decided.  The group `[13,13,13,12,13,13,13,13]` closed at exactly
# 23 when `8,8` landed at 3082.8, and the very next row was
# group this header had already named, and the first of the fourteen
# members it had already listed.**  `12,11,3` followed at 6342.8, so
# **2 of 14 are in hand and none is outside the permitted set.**
# `12,11,3` COST 6342.8, WHICH IS 1.74x THE RUNNING MEDIAN, and this is
# recorded as a fact and NOT read.  The eleven labels before it ran
# 3258.5, 3082.8, 3348.7 -- a tight band -- and the median over the
# earlier 153 labels is 3648.8.  So the new group's first two, 3348.7
# and 6342.8, are already a wider spread than the whole of the previous
# group's tail.  **NOTHING IS CONCLUDED FROM TWO POINTS.**  If this
# group is systematically dearer it will show over its 14 members, and
# the standing abstention on cost is not being revised to notice a
# single expensive row -- that is the exact move this file has withdrawn
# five times.  Both members decided on their FIRST attempt.
# Two things were predicted here and both held: WHICH GROUP comes next,
# and WHICH TAILS it admits.  Neither is a claim about difficulty and
# neither is a result about sunflowers -- both are arithmetic about what
# the encoding permits, checked by generating the set and comparing.
# **THE PREDICTION RESOLVES, AND IT WAS PUT WHERE IT COULD FAIL.**  One
# row ago this header said `8,8` was the single most-checkable claim it
# had left, and that if the group closed at anything other than exactly
# `8,8` the encoding argument was wrong.  Generating the whole permitted
# `w + x + y = 25` and `13 >= w >= x >= y >= 0` -- and comparing it
# against the banked labels as SETS:
#     permitted members      23
#     landed members         23
#     landed but not permitted   NONE
#     permitted but not landed   NONE
# Five sub-families, 7 + 6 + 5 + 3 + 2 = 23.  This is the one kind of
# claim in this file that has never failed, and the reason is worth
# repeating rather than celebrating: it is arithmetic about what the
# ENCODING permits, not a fit to any measured curve.  Every reading of
# the observed cost curve in this file has been withdrawn; every reading
# of the generator has held.  What it demonstrates is that the block
# constraints are understood correctly, which is worth having and is not
# a result about sunflowers.
# `w = 10` arrived in descending-`x` order (10, 9, 8).  Recorded as WHAT
# HAPPENED and not as a return to form: the sub-family before it did
# not, three earlier families did not, and this file no longer claims
# arrival order is predictable in either direction.  Two in-order
# families in a row is exactly the evidence that produced the sixteenth
# withdrawal, and it is not being read a second time.  The `w = 11` sub-family has `11,3` at 2821.4, `10,4` at
# `8,6` was never missing, only slow: it landed 10 m 16 s after `7,7`
# overtook it, and its 3692.7 s is the family's LARGEST cost, which is
# the whole of the explanation.  The membership prediction is five for
# five and the sub-family is CLOSED by arithmetic: block 2 admits
# exactly `x = 11,10,9,8,7` at `w = 11` and nothing else.
# **THAT BREAKS A PHRASE THIS HEADER HAS USED REPEATEDLY, AND THE PHRASE
# WAS ALWAYS AN OVERSTATEMENT.**  Every batch since the second family
# opened has said the members landed "in the predicted order".  The
# prediction was about MEMBERSHIP -- which tails the encoding permits --
# and said nothing about arrival order, which is set by four solvers
# finishing at different times, not by the enumeration.  The first two
# families did arrive strictly in order (checked: x ran 12,11,10,9,8,7,6
# and 12,11,10,9,8,7), and that was scheduling luck being read as
# confirmation of something never claimed.  `7,7` finished in 2933.8 s
# while `8,6` was still running, so it landed first; `8,6` came in ten
# minutes later at 3692.7, the largest cost in the family.
# **AND IT WAS NOT THE FIRST TIME -- THIS FILE ALREADY HELD THREE
# COUNTEREXAMPLES WHILE THE PHRASE WAS IN USE.**  Scripting arrival order
# across ALL 36 families that have two or more members in hand finds three
# that arrived out of descending-`x` order well before this one:
# (Ordinals only, deliberately: these are permanent facts about arrival
# position, and pinning a "of N labels" denominator to them would go
# stale on the next row -- which is the failure this section is about.
# The w = 11 family above is itself the fourth such case, at 143.)
# The first violator family -- the only kind the phrase was ever applied
# to -- was the 127th label, so the earliest counterexample had been in
# this file for 39 labels before the phrase was first written.
# All three are globally sorted -- NON-violator families -- and "in the
# predicted order" was only ever said of the violator families, where it
# did hold.  The phrase was therefore checked against the slice that
# prompted it and never against the rest of the file, which had already
# refuted the general property three times over.
# That makes this a DIFFERENT failure from the block-sortedness one, and
# the difference is the useful part.  There the counterexample did not yet
# exist: 215 rows agreed and row 216 was the first that could have
# disagreed.  Here the counterexamples were sitting in this same file the
# whole time, one script away, and were missed because the claim was only
# ever run against the rows it was about.  **When a regularity shows up in
# a slice, the cheapest test is the rest of the data already in hand.**
# **AND THE CHECK FOR ALL OF THE ABOVE WAS ITSELF WRONG, WHICH IS THE
# PART WORTH KEEPING.**  The script that verified these numbers reported
# `89 UNSAT, 57 UNKNOWN` against a header saying `146 UNSAT, 0 UNKNOWN`
# (the counts as they then stood, at 146 labels).
# The HEADER was right.  Getting arrival order requires keeping each
# label's FIRST row, so the script was built first-write-wins -- and that
# silently redefined the status tally from "how each label stands now" to
# "how each label came back on attempt one".  Both are real quantities;
# only one is what STANDING means.  Taken at face value it would have
# converted a correct header into a wrong one, in the name of verifying
# it.  **A check that disagrees with the thing it checks has two
# suspects, and the newer code is the better bet.**  Resolved by
# computing first-, last- and any-UNSAT per label side by side: last and
# any-UNSAT agreed with each other and with the header, and no label has
# ever regressed from UNSAT.
# The wrong reading is a real statistic under its correct name, and it
# has not been stated in this file before: **57 of the 154 decided
# labels -- 37.0% -- were NOT decided on their first attempt**, and all
# 57 were later banked by a re-run or a cap raise.  97 fell first time.
# (This ratio moves with every row; it is quoted as of 154 labels.  The
# numerator is frozen: **the last 41 labels have every one of them
# fallen on their first attempt**, so 57 was fixed 36 labels ago and
# the percentage is drifting down purely on its denominator.  This
# sentence first said "seven rows", typed from impression; the script
# said 36.  The straggler era is over as a matter of record, not of
# expectation -- and no claim is made that it stays over, since the
# enumeration has just entered the 92% it had never touched.)
# The membership prediction is untouched -- `7,7` is a predicted member
# and `8,6` remains outstanding -- and this is recorded because a claim
# that quietly grows extra content between batches is exactly what
# 54.3a is for.  See the violator section:
# counting the enumeration directly shows violators are 92% of this
# cube, not a curiosity.
# **AND THE HEADLINE IS THAT ONE COHORT OF FOUR WENT FOUR FOR FOUR.**
# The four solvers launched together at ~04:13 all decided their cubes,
# in order, at 7497.4, 7838.8, 8270.4 and 8900.8 s of their own runtime
# -- every one clear of the 10800 s cap, by 3302, 2961, 2529 and 1899 s.
# Predicted finish times from a 04:13:50 start are 06:18:47, 06:24:28,
# 06:43, which is how the cohort was identified rather than guessed at.
# These were not easy cubes held back: the four carried **eighteen prior
# stalls between them** (2, 4, 6 and 6), almost all within 120 s of the
# cap.
# **THE OBVIOUS EXPLANATION IS ALREADY CONTRADICTED BY THIS FILE.**  The
# natural story is that a freshly restarted container solves faster --
# this cohort began 71 s after the tenth restart.  But the cohort
# launched at ~22:06, 60 s after the NINTH restart, went 2 of 4 and both
# of its wins were near-cap (10053.0, 10270.3).  Same relationship to a
# restart, very different outcome, so post-restart freshness does not
# account for it.  No replacement mechanism is offered: this file records
# WALL time and not solver-side time, so "the machine was faster" and
# "the search was luckier" cannot be separated from these rows at all.
# What is left is a statement about variance rather than about cubes:
# **cohort-to-cohort variation here is far larger than the per-label
# variation the marginal-instance reading assumed**, and four successes
# arriving together are worth much less than four arriving apart.
# the old 5400 s cap and then five times at the 10800 s cap
# **UNSAT at 10053.0**, under the cap and below every one of its own
# stalls.  Minutes later `[13,13,13,13,13,13,12,11,11,9,7]` did the same
# on its sixth attempt -- five stalls at 10860-10900, then **UNSAT at
# 10270.3**.  Eight stragglers remain, all at run>=12 = 7 except one at
# **AND THE RE-RUN YIELD'S NUMERATOR MOVED TWICE, HAVING NEVER MOVED
# BEFORE: 5 of 29 repeats = 0.17.**  One batch ago this header made a
# point of the fact that the numerator had never left three and that
# every revision -- 0.37, 0.18, 0.14, 0.13, 0.11 -- came from the
# denominator growing.  That is no longer true, and the estimate went UP
# twice inside one batch.
# **A SPLIT WRITTEN AND THEN BROKEN BY THE NEXT ROW, BEFORE IT WAS EVEN
# COMMITTED.**  With the first of the two rows in hand, repeats
# following a 10800 s stall looked like this, by leading run of degrees
#     run>=12 = 8    8 repeats, 4 decided     0.50
#     run>=12 <= 7  20 repeats, 0 decided     0.00
# and this header wrote it up, with the caveat that **0 of 20 does not
# establish a rate of zero -- by the rule of three the 95% upper bound
# on that arm is about 3/20 = 0.15, which comfortably contains the
# pooled rate.**  The second row landed minutes later, before the commit,
# and it was a run>=12 = 7 label.  The current table:
#     run>=12 = 8    8 repeats, 4 decided     0.500
#     run>=12 <= 7  31 repeats, 9 decided     0.290
#     pooled        39 repeats, 13 decided    0.333   <- the header figure
# **The caveat was vindicated within a single row.**  Two claims from
# the first version are dead: that the second arm's rate is zero, and
# that every open straggler sits in an arm that has never produced a
# success.  What survives is weaker and is all that was ever supportable:
# the two arms' point estimates differ by about a factor of three on 8
# and 26 repeats, which is suggestive and is not a demonstrated
# difference.  **THE GAP HAS NOW CLOSED NINE TIMES RUNNING, ON NINE
# CONSECUTIVE ROWS: ten, six, four, three, 2.7, 2.3, 2.1, 1.9, now
# 1.7.**  Every repeat this run will ever make is now behind it, so this
# is the final reading: 4 of 8 against 9 of 31.
# Every one of those moves came from the LOWER arm gaining a success,
# and the upper arm has not gained a repeat since it emptied.  A ratio
# that shrinks monotonically as the sample grows is the signature 54.3a's
# second check names -- it is measuring the smallness of the sample, not
# a property of the cubes.  **Do not quote the ratio.**  The honest
# statement is that 4 of 8 and 4 of 26 are both consistent with the
# pooled 0.235 and with each other, and that on this trajectory the
# split will read as no difference at all within a few more rows.
# The composition point does survive, because it does not depend on the
# rates: **all four of the run>=12 = 8 stragglers have now been decided**,
# so that arm is empty going forward and the pooled 0.17 is measured on a
# population that no longer exists.  Every remaining straggler is at
# run>=12 <= 7.  Do not carry 0.17 forward as the expected yield of the
# remaining sweep -- but do not carry 0.048 forward either, on one
# success in twenty-one.
# A READING MADE BY EYE AND KILLED BY SCRIPT, in the same batch.  The
# four successes all begin `13,13,13,13,13,13,12,12`, and that looked
# like the pattern.  It is not: the decided-after-stalling labels run
# through many prefixes, and the variable that actually separates them
# is run>=12.  The prefix reading was an artefact of looking only at the
# four successes instead of at every label that ever stalled.
# A CONFOUND FOUND AND REMOVED, WHICH CUT A HEADLINE NUMBER BY 70%.
# Counting every label that ever stalled and was later decided gives 45
# of 45 at run>=12 >= 8, which is a striking number and a misleading
# one: **41 of those 45 stalled only at the OLD 5400 s cap** and were
# decided by the raise to 10800, not by a repeat.  Restricted to labels
# that stalled at the CURRENT cap the comparison is 4 of 4 against 0 of
# 9 -- thirteen labels, not fifty-seven.  The 45-of-45 version would
# have been the twelfth withdrawal.
# WINDOWS at 251 rows: ALL attempts 8 of 8 and 12 of 12; FIRST attempts
# 8 of 8 and 12 of 12.  The raise stays unarmed under either (condition
# is 0 or 1 banked in twelve, and the worse reading is 6).  Never raise
# off a window the resume policy filled: the all-attempts window has now
# spent ALL TWELVE of its last twelve slots on straggler repeats, and the
# first-attempts window -- which is the one that says anything about the
# frontier -- has not moved off a clean sweep since it was introduced.
# (Housekeeping, recorded rather than silently fixed: this block until
# now ended with the sentence "The 8-window is 5 of 8 and the 12-window
# 5 of 12; both say hold and the earlier disagreement is closed."  That
# was stale text from an earlier batch, left in place while the sentence
# above it was updated, and the two flatly contradicted each other.  A
# recount over all 228 rows gave 8 of 8 and 12 of 12 -- a reading of
# THAT batch, superseded one batch later when four straggler repeats
# landed; see the standing block above for the current pair.  I have not tried
# to establish which batch the 5-of-8 reading was true for; the point of
# recording it is that a header edited in place accumulates sentences
# that were each true once, and only a recount distinguishes them.)
# **THE RESUME HAS NOW RE-RUN ALL TEN STRAGGLERS AND DECIDED NONE OF
# THEM.**  That is the complete cycle, not a sample of it: every label
# this run carried as UNKNOWN was given a fresh 10800 s and every one
# came back UNKNOWN.  Cost, ten attempts at ~10900 s on four threads,
# about 7.6 wall-hours.  It is the price the resume policy charges after
# each container restart, and it is now measured rather than estimated.
# **THE 8-vs-12 WINDOW TEST IS RESOLVED, AND THE 12-WINDOW WAS RIGHT.**
# This is the one prediction in this file that was written down BEFORE
# its outcome, so it is the only one whose verdict is not a
# rationalisation.
# Recorded at 207 rows, with the two windows disagreeing for the first
# time in the session:
#     last  8 attempts   0 UNSAT / 8    0.00 UNSAT/h   <- raise trigger
#     last 12 attempts   4 UNSAT / 12   0.60 UNSAT/h   <- hold
# The rule says use the 12 and it said HOLD.  Two rows later:
#     last  8 attempts   2 UNSAT / 8    0.38 UNSAT/h   <- no longer zero
#     last 12 attempts   4 UNSAT / 12   0.57 UNSAT/h   <- still hold
# Had the raise fired on the 8-window it would have doubled the cap to
